messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mariana had spent three decades as a detective, but nothing prepared her for the call that Saturday evening—a clandestine drug lab explosion in a warehouse on the south side. She arrived before the hazmat team, pushing through a crowd of panicked neighbors to reach a collapsed wall. A cloud of acrid fumes hit her as she knelt to check for survivors; her lungs seized, and she gasped, tasting something metallic and chemical. She felt her own sweat pooling under her vest, the sour smell mixing with the burning plastic. A paramedic later guided her to an ambulance, where the sterile antiseptic and latex gloves burned into her memory. That night in the emergency room, the doctors told her the chemicals were unstable but she would recover. Mariana did breathe again, but not the way she used to. In the weeks that followed, she found herself ducking into doorways whenever she heard a sudden bang—a truck backfiring, a dropped metal tray in the precinct break room. Her body stayed tense, her shoulders knotted, her eyes darting across the parking lot before she got out of her car. What frightened her most was the way the hospital smell would catch her off guard. The first time she walked past a clinic, her throat tightened, and she had to cover her face with both hands, forcing herself to think of the grocery list instead. Even a colleague’s sweat after a morning run made her stomach drop and her mind leap back to that warehouse floor, but only in jagged pieces—a flash of a chemical drum, the paramedic’s glove, the cold oxygen mask—never the whole thing. She had come to believe that she would never feel normal emotions again, that her body would always be this coiled, that the department that sent her in without proper gear had failed her entirely. Once she was convinced that the world and her own body were no longer safe, nearly every ordinary sound or smell became a trigger — a car backfiring, a whiff of bleach, a colleague's aftershave — because her appraisals had turned the everyday into a landscape of potential threats. That belief kept her tethered to the explosion scene, as if her mind needed to revisit the exact moment where normal ended, so the memory stayed close and vivid. That last belief made her flinch every time she saw a uniform, so she started avoiding the squad room, taking paperwork home, speaking only to her partner through text. The connections tightened into a loop she could not name. A sudden sound put her on high alert and, at the same time, shoved a fragmented memory into her throat; she blocked it before it finished, and the very act of blocking convinced her she was losing control of her own mind. The more she believed she had to be on guard all the time, the more she scanned the hallway for shadows, and the more she scanned, the more breathless she became when she caught the faintest hint of a cleaning product. That breathlessness sent her straight to her old redirection trick—picturing her daughter’s graduation—but the trick also reinforced her sense that the memory was too dangerous to face. She had started hiding her face at her desk whenever a nurse’s perfume drifted by, and in those moments the event felt present again, not over. Each time she pushed the memory away, the negative appraisal that she was permanently broken grew stronger, and that appraisal made her avoid not only smells but also authority figures: she no longer attended briefings with the captain, citing a stomach bug. But that blocking had the unintended effect of keeping the memory intact and unprocessed, so that when it next surfaced it arrived with a force she could not counter — all that suppression had preserved it in full. Her work suffered—she missed a deadline on a burglary case—and her partner gently asked if she was okay. She said she was fine, but she was certain she was not. What finally brought Mariana to seek help was a piece of evidence: a forensic photo from a new case, a chemical spill at a manufacturing plant. The image alone triggered a surge of breathlessness so intense she thought she would black out. She drove herself to the precinct’s employee assistance office, her hands shaking on the wheel. What she hoped for was to stop the loop—to be able to walk into the break room without covering her face, to hear a door slam without her heart racing. But what she feared most was that the loop would not break, that the institutional failure she blamed would never be fixed, and that the woman who used to lead scenes would remain fractured, always on guard, always bracing for a trigger she could not predict. Each time a trigger struck like that, it drove the conviction deeper that she would never feel normal again and that her body was permanently wired for alarm.
